exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents 3 months postpartum with inability to breast‑feed and amenorrhoea; what is the next investigation and why? — Check early morning cortisol to rule out adrenal insufficiency before any other test.

During a labour emergency you note massive bleeding; what prophylactic measure could prevent Sheehan syndrome? — Prompt volume resuscitation and blood transfusion to maintain perfusion to the pituitary.

A patient with known Sheehan syndrome is scheduled for emergency C‑section; how should her steroid regimen be managed? — Give stress‑dose IV hydrocortisone before induction, then continue oral replacement post‑operatively.
What clinical sign distinguishes Sheehan syndrome from primary hypothyroidism? — Low/normal TSH with low free T4 versus high TSH in primary disease.

A postpartum woman complains of fatigue and cold intolerance; labs show low cortisol and low free T4; why must glucocorticoids be started before levothyroxine? — Thyroid hormone increases metabolism and can precipitate adrenal crisis if cortisol is insufficient.

Explain why menstrual irregularities may appear months after delivery in Sheehan syndrome. — Gonadotropin (LH/FSH) deficiency develops as pituitary necrosis progresses, leading to secondary amenorrhoea.
What complication is most likely if estrogen replacement is omitted in a young woman with Sheehan syndrome? — Early osteoporosis and increased fracture risk.

How does the presentation of pituitary apoplexy differ from Sheehan syndrome? — Apoplexy presents with sudden severe headache, visual field loss, and possible ophthalmoplegia, while Sheehan is painless and follows haemorrhage.
ai.title: Sheehan Syndrome
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Sheehan syndrome is ischemic necrosis of the pituitary gland after massive postpartum hemorrhage. It produces varying degrees of anterior pituitary hormone deficiency, often presenting months later with failure to lactate, amenorrhoea and fatigue.

b: Absence of lactation within 48 h of delivery
Low serum cortisol, TSH, LH/FSH, prolactin
sections.p: Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary occurring after severe postpartum haemorrhage, diagnosed by clinical hormone deficits and imaging when available.

b: Stage 1: Isolated prolactin deficiency (failure to lactate)
Stage 2: Additional gonadotropin deficiency (amenorrhoea, infertility)
Stage 3: Thyroid and adrenal axis involvement (cold intolerance, hypotension, hypoglycaemia)
Stage 4: Full pan‑hypopituitarism with severe fatigue, hyponatraemia, and possible adrenal crisis
sections.p: Severity is graded by the number of hormone axes affected and the degree of functional loss.

b: Severe postpartum haemorrhage (most common)
Hypovolemic shock with hypotension
Coagulopathy (e.g., disseminated intravascular coagulation)
Concurrent infections (malaria, sepsis) that worsen shock
sections.p: The primary cause is acute pituitary hypoperfusion during massive obstetric haemorrhage.

b: Failure to produce milk despite intact nipples
Secondary amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea
Fatigue, loss of libido, dry skin
Cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation (central hypothyroidism)
Hypoglycaemia, dizziness, low blood pressure (secondary adrenal insufficiency)
Anemia and low libido due to low ACTH and gonadotropins
sections.p: Symptoms evolve from the immediate postpartum period to months later, reflecting loss of each hormone.
Targeted hormone assays and imaging confirm the diagnosis; alternatives are given when tests are unavailable.

t.b: Is adrenal axis intact? Low cortisol suggests secondary adrenal insufficiency; if unavailable, assess for hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia.
Is thyroid axis affected? Low free T4 with normal/low TSH indicates central hypothyroidism; if labs missing, look for cold intolerance and bradycardia.
Is lactotroph function lost? Very low prolactin supports diagnosis; if not measurable, rely on clinical failure to lactate.
Assess gonadal axis; low values explain amenorrhoea; if unavailable, note menstrual history.
Shows an empty sella or pituitary shrinkage; when unavailable, diagnosis rests on clinical picture and hormone profile.

b: Acute adrenal crisis: severe hypotension, vomiting, abdominal pain, altered mental status
Severe hyponatraemia leading to seizures
Hypoglycaemic coma
Cardiovascular collapse during surgery or infection
Infertility and poor bone health from chronic estrogen deficiency
sections.p: Unrecognised adrenal insufficiency can precipitate crisis; other complications arise from chronic hormone deficits.

b: Start glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone or equivalent) before any thyroid hormone to avoid precipitating crisis
Add levothyroxine once cortisol coverage is adequate; monitor for tachycardia
Introduce estrogen‑progesterone therapy for women desiring fertility or to prevent osteoporosis
Consider growth‑hormone replacement only in selected cases (rare in low‑resource settings)
Treat underlying anemia, infections, and provide iron or folate as needed
Educate on stress‑dosing of steroids during illness or surgery
sections.p: Replace deficient hormones in order of physiological urgency, treat precipitating factors, and educate the patient.

b: Quarterly clinical review of weight, blood pressure, menstrual status, and lactation ability
Annual serum cortisol, free T4, and gonadotropins; adjust doses accordingly
Bone mineral density screening after 5 years of estrogen deficiency
Counselling on safe childbirth practices, early recognition of postpartum haemorrhage, and timely blood transfusion
Community education on the importance of skilled birth attendance
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring of hormone levels and clinical status prevents crises and improves quality of life.

b: Post‑partum pituitary apoplexy – sudden severe headache and visual loss; Sheehan is usually painless and follows haemorrhage
Primary hypothyroidism – high TSH, unlike low/normal TSH in Sheehan
Hyperprolactinaemia from pituitary adenoma – high prolactin, not low
sections.p: Conditions that also cause lactation failure or amenorrhoea after delivery.

b: TSH can be normal or low in central hypothyroidism, giving a false sense of euthyroidism
Serum sodium may be normal early in adrenal insufficiency; hyponatraemia appears later
Prolactin may be modestly elevated in stress, masking low baseline levels
sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite significant deficiency.

ai.clinicalScope: Post‑partum hypopituitarism (Sheehan syndrome) in women after severe obstetric hemorrhage, especially in low‑resource East African hospitals
whenToSeekHelp: Sudden collapse, severe vomiting, or confusion after a stressful event (possible adrenal crisis)
Persistent low blood pressure despite fluids
